rv.q: Sure, the narrative becomes a bit of a cluster-muck in the second act — but mostly it’s just screamingly good fun.
That enthusiasm translates to the audience, too, with every visual reference lifted directly from the movie yielding huge laughs.
It’s also—thanks in large part to Alex Brightman’s spot-on performance as the incorrigible titular ghoul—a pretty fun time.
This reworked incarnation breathes slightly more enjoyably even as it remains too faithful to the pumped-up inclinations.
Beetlejuice runs itself ragged for less.
It never quite finds the right mixture of funny and creepy, lurid and light.
If only so much of the rest of Beetlejuice were not a busy mess.
The disheartening moral of “Beetlejuice” is that when anything goes, nothing much registers in the end.

The major impression, ultimately, is not that of a clever romp wickedly testing the limits of the tasteless, but of a repetitive refrain of disgust and disdain—not only for the imagined beings onstage, but for those still in the land of the living, buying the tickets.
Truly, this is most cacophonous and ill-conceived musical of the season— in fact, for several seasons.
Fresh off his heinous music for “King Kong,” the Australian composer’s dismal soft-rock score fuels one of the worst Broadway musicals in years.
I’m at a loss to describe it except to say it left me with a headache no Excedrin can cure.
Brightman’s performance is dead-on, so to speak.
High-spirited fun, wickedly good tunes and eye-popping visuals make this night of the living dead a scream.
And if this Beetlejuice has a flaw, it’s that: In its insistence on entertaining you, it’s a story about death with tons of life but maybe not quite as much soul.
Beetlejuice, as it now presents itself, is a loopy, nutty, loud, winning hoot.
For all the talent here, the show suffers from sensory overload.

All three are exquisite — corpses and all. Nathan Lane stars in ‘Gary: A Sequel to Titus Andronicus’ on Broadway. This is a comedic look at the gruesome side of death by way of existential humor — a mixture of Beckett, commedia dell'arte, Theatre of the Ridiculous and more — that won't sit well with some.

Still, if you can tolerate the bombardment, and don’t mind sappy scenes mixed in with the comically macabre plot, Beetlejuice the musical does have its pleasures – principally a few standout performances and especially the vivid visuals.
Beetlejuice isn’t worthy to shine the earlier musical’s singing-and-dancing shoes.
And it's yet another charmless, dumbed-down musical adaptation of a well-known movie, just like the others that have premiered in recent months (including “Pretty Woman,” “King Kong” and “Tootsie”).
“Beetlejuice” the musical suffers from a severe case of rigor mortis.
A fun house with nothing shoring it up; its attractions provide scant amusement.
Beetlejuice is full throttled riotous fun, and shouldn’t be missed, whether a fan of the movie, or not.
It’s a whole lot of ghoulish fun.
What remains pretty constant is the playful obnoxiousness and energy of Alex Brightman as Beetlejuice.
The musical adaptation is a visual feast that captures the gothic whimsy of the original.
The show holds nothing back and all in all, Beetlejuice offers sane advice about living life to the fullest.
For all the show’s relentlessly hellsapoppin’ antics, you’ll need a youthful spirit to fully appreciate them.
What’s on stage now at the Winter Garden is among the most frenetic offerings ever seen on Broadway.
Beetlejuice is a Broadway crowd pleaser that does what it sets out to do: provide a visually pleasing reminder of an old favorite.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this manic musical adaptation: fans praise Alex Brightman's energetic performance and eye-popping visuals, while detractors find it exhaustingly loud, tonally confused, and crass.
